intro.heading: The policy says "the lead". Half the team guess who that is.
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: A deputy manager is reading through the policy folder with a cup of tea. Every policy names a role: the safeguarding lead, the infection prevention and control lead, the Caldicott Guardian, the fire safety officer. None of them names a person. Last spring someone changed role, and nobody went back through the documents. At handover a new carer asks who the safeguarding lead is, and two senior staff give two different answers. The policies are sound. They simply do not say who holds each job today. Here is how that plays out.

trail.text: The policies are written and approved, with each role named by title.
New staff are told to read the policies and sign the folder.
Everyone agrees roles and responsibilities are clear.
The lead for one role moves on. The documents do not change.
Another lead is picked up by a different senior. Only some staff hear.
A carer asks who to tell. Two seniors name two people.
Sound policies, but no one place showing who holds each role.
"Who is your safeguarding lead?" The team is not sure.

trail_close: Nobody did anything wrong. The names simply lived in people's heads instead of one place the policies could read from. Here is why that matters, and how to fix it.

why.heading: A role on paper only helps if people know who holds it
why.sub: Staff follow what the policy says. If it points to a title, they have to work out the person.

cards.title: Staff ask the person next to them
cards.body: When a policy says "tell the lead", a worried carer asks a colleague. That colleague may be out of date. A named person removes the guesswork.

cards.title: One place to keep names current
cards.body: Updating a name in each of your care home policies by hand is slow and easy to miss. Keeping role holders in one list means a change is made once.

cards.title: Changes slip through quietly
cards.body: People move roles, go on leave or leave the service. Without a prompt to check, an out of date name can sit in a policy for months.

how.heading: Name the role once. Let the policies and the team follow.

Staff open it in the Staff Hub. Questions are built from your own policies where they cover the topic.
Short and practical, so it fits a handover, not a training day. This mock is an illustration.

talk.heading: What managers ask about naming leads
talk.sub: Plain answers, including what the product does not do.

items.q: How do I name a lead in CareStream?
items.a: In Settings you assign a staff member to a named role. CareStream supports 24 named roles, and you can also type a name in by hand if the person is not on your staff list.

items.q: Will the name appear in my policies?
items.a: Where a policy mentions the role, the name is shown instead of the bare title. This merge is part of the Professional and Enterprise plans, and a switch turns it off if you prefer titles.

items.q: Does it change my policies by itself when someone moves on?
items.a: No. Changing the role holder in Settings updates the name that is shown. It does not rewrite your policy wording, and any suggested policy fix stays a suggestion until an admin adopts it and your approval steps finish.

items.q: Can I check that staff actually know who the leads are?
items.a: Yes. Assign a short module on named role holders in Adhoc Training. A wrong answer becomes a follow up the person opens with Learn and retry, and you see the pattern in Knowledge gaps.
It is one of the 24 named roles, so you can name the person. We do not define or advise on the role itself. Your own governance arrangements and official guidance come first.

items.q: Does it record that staff have read the policy?
items.a: It records read sessions, such as time spent and scroll, and a Mark as read action. It does not hold signatures or a policy version number against each read.

items.q: Does it tell me if a policy has no one named?
items.a: Gap checking looks at coverage, consistency and out of date wording, not who is named. If nobody is assigned a role, the policy keeps the plain role title.

items.q: What does it cost and can I try it?
items.a: There is a 14 day free trial on the paid plans. Create a free account to look around, and see the pricing page for current plan details.

cards.title: It does not pick the right person
cards.body: You decide who holds each role. CareStream shows the name you set. It does not check qualifications, training or whether someone is suited to a role.

cards.title: It does not rewrite your policies for you
cards.body: Names are shown where a policy mentions a role. Wording changes are suggestions until an admin adopts them and your approval chain finishes. Nothing is edited behind your back.

cards.title: It is not legal advice or a guarantee
cards.body: It helps you keep policy compliance visible. It does not promise compliance or a CQC rating, and it does not tell you who must hold a role in your service.

faqs.heading: Questions about named leads and policies

items.q: What does a lead do for safeguarding in a care home?
items.a: That is set by your own policy and local arrangements, so we do not define it here. Our safeguarding policy guide explains how a policy should describe the role.

The UK Caldicott Guardian Council describes it as a senior person responsible for protecting the confidentiality of people's health and care information. CareStream lets you name that person among your role holders.

items.q: Who should be the policy owner for each policy?
items.a: That is your decision. Many services give each policy an owner who reviews it. CareStream shows named role holders in your policies, and our guide to reviewing policies covers review habits.

items.q: Can one person hold more than one role?
items.a: Yes, nothing stops the same person being named for several roles. Think about whether that is workable when they are away.

items.q: How does this help with policy governance?
items.a: It keeps names in one place and lets you check staff know them. Good policy governance also needs review dates, approval and version history, which sit in the policy features on Professional and above.

items.q: Can I name role holders on the Starter plan?
items.a: Role holder names merged into policies is a Professional and Enterprise feature. Check the pricing page for what each plan includes today.

items.q: Do I need to update every one of my care home policies when a lead changes?
items.a: No. Change the role holder in Settings and policies that name the role show the new name where the merge is switched on. Your version control habits still matter for wording changes.
It checks policies for gaps, conflicts and out of date wording. See policy gap detection. Final decisions on compliance stay with you.

guide.heading: A simple way to keep named leads current
guide.lede: You do not need new systems to start. A short routine does most of the work.

sections.h3: List the roles your service actually uses
paragraphs: Start from the roles your policies mention, not from a long list. Under Regulation 17 of the 2014 regulations, providers must operate systems and processes effectively and keep necessary records about the management of the regulated activity. Knowing who holds each lead role is a sensible part of that picture, though the regulation does not name specific roles.
checklist: Write down every role title your policies mention
Name one person for each, and a cover if you can
Tell the team where the list lives
Set a date to check the list each quarter

paragraphs: A name on a list is not the same as staff knowing it. A short question at handover, or a Staff Hub module on named role holders, shows you quickly who is unsure. Read the answers as a prompt to brief people, not as a score.
When a lead leaves, changes role or goes on long leave, update the name the same day and let the team know. Our guide to policy drift lists other signs your policy set needs attention.

guide.note: This guide is general information for managers. It is not legal advice. Check your own responsibilities with the relevant regulator and guidance.
